title.en: MTEB Leaderboard: Choosing the Right Embedding Model

description.en: Learn how to read the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard and pick the right embedding model for your RAG system by balancing accuracy, size, latency, and dimension cost.

story_variants.en:
## The Leaderboard That Picks Your Embedder

Vaathiyaar leans over your shoulder as you scroll through Hugging Face. "Stop," he says. "Before you write a single line of RAG code, answer one question: *which embedding model?* Get this wrong and no amount of clever prompting will save you â€” garbage retrieval means garbage answers. Luckily, the community already built the answer key. It's called **MTEB**: the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark."

### What MTEB Actually Measures

MTEB evaluates embedding models across **hundreds of datasets** grouped into task categories: Retrieval, Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), Classification, Clustering, Reranking, and more. The leaderboard at `mteb/leaderboard` on Hugging Face Spaces ranks models by their average score â€” but the average is a trap.

"If you're building RAG," Vaathiyaar warns, "the **Retrieval** column matters far more than the overall average. A model can ace classification and still fetch terrible passages."

### The Real Trade-off Table

| Model | MTEB Avg | Params | Dim | Runs on CPU? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| all-MiniLM-L6-v2 | ~56 | 22M | 384 | Yes, fast |
| bge-base-en-v1.5 | ~64 | 109M | 768 | Yes |
| gte-large-en-v1.5 | ~65 | 434M | 1024 | Slow |
| e5-mistral-7b-instruct | ~67 | 7B | 4096 | No (GPU) |

Notice the pattern: **each point of MTEB score gets exponentially more expensive**. Going from 56 â†’ 64 costs you 5Ã— the parameters. Going from 65 â†’ 67 costs a GPU and 4096-dim vectors that quadruple your vector-database storage bill.

### Scoring Models Programmatically

"Never eyeball a leaderboard when you can code the decision," says Vaathiyaar.

```python
candidates = {
    "all-MiniLM-L6-v2":  {"retrieval": 41.9, "params_m": 22,   "dim": 384},
    "bge-base-en-v1.5":  {"retrieval": 53.2, "params_m": 109,  "dim": 768},
    "e5-mistral-7b":     {"retrieval": 56.9, "params_m": 7110, "dim": 4096},
}

def pick(candidates, max_params_m):
    ok = {n: c for n, c in candidates.items() if c["params_m"] <= max_params_m}
    return max(ok, key=lambda n: ok[n]["retrieval"])

print(pick(candidates, 200))  # bge-base-en-v1.5
```

Three lines of filtering beat an afternoon of leaderboard-scrolling. Constrain by what your hardware allows, *then* maximize the metric your application actually uses.

### The Homie Rule of Thumb

For a local-first assistant like Homie, the decision tree is short: if it must run on CPU alongside everything else, a 22Mâ€“109M parameter model is the ceiling. `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` embeds thousands of sentences per second on a laptop; `bge-base-en-v1.5` buys ~11 retrieval points for a still-tolerable slowdown. The 7B giants only make sense when a GPU is guaranteed and storage is cheap.

> **Key Insight:** The best embedding model is not the one at the top of the MTEB leaderboard â€” it's the highest-scoring model *on your task category* that fits your latency, memory, and vector-storage budget. Filter first, then rank.

content.en: **Vaathiyaar:** "Every RAG system lives or dies by its embedder. MTEB â€” the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark â€” is the community's answer key. Today you'll learn to read it like an engineer: filter by constraints first, rank by the right column second."

animation_sequence.code:
candidates = {
    "all-MiniLM-L6-v2":  {"retrieval": 41.9, "params_m": 22,   "dim": 384},
    "bge-base-en-v1.5":  {"retrieval": 53.2, "params_m": 109,  "dim": 768},
    "gte-large-en-v1.5": {"retrieval": 57.9, "params_m": 434,  "dim": 1024},
    "e5-mistral-7b":     {"retrieval": 56.9, "params_m": 7110, "dim": 4096},
}

MAX_PARAMS_M = 200
MAX_DIM = 1024

affordable = {n: c for n, c in candidates.items()
              if c["params_m"] <= MAX_PARAMS_M and c["dim"] <= MAX_DIM}

best = max(affordable, key=lambda n: affordable[n]["retrieval"])

storage_gb = affordable[best]["dim"] * 4 * 1_000_000 / 1e9
print(f"Ship: {best} ({storage_gb:.1f} GB per 1M vectors)")

explanation.en: We start with a shortlist pulled from the MTEB leaderboard. Each entry records the Retrieval score (the column that matters for RAG), parameter count in millions, and embedding dimension.
all-MiniLM-L6-v2: only 22M parameters and 384-dim vectors. The baseline that runs anywhere â€” even a Raspberry Pi.
gte-large-en-v1.5 scores higher on Retrieval than models 16Ã— its size â€” leaderboard rank by *average* would have hidden this.
e5-mistral-7b: a 7-billion-parameter giant producing 4096-dim vectors. Top of the average leaderboard, but look at the cost.
Now we encode our real-world constraints as code. Homie must run on CPU, so we cap parameters at 200M.
Dimension caps matter too: every extra dimension multiplies vector-database storage and similarity-search latency.
Filter FIRST. A dict comprehension keeps only models that satisfy both hardware constraints â€” the giants drop out before we ever rank.
Rank SECOND. max() with a key function picks the highest Retrieval score among survivors. Note: not the highest average â€” the highest score on OUR task.
Engineers think in bills: dim Ã— 4 bytes (float32) Ã— 1M chunks. A 768-dim model needs ~3 GB per million vectors; 4096-dim would need ~16 GB.
Final answer: bge-base-en-v1.5 â€” the best retriever that actually fits the deployment. The leaderboard informed the decision; constraints made it.

message.en: You can now read MTEB like an engineer â€” filter by constraints, rank by task. Homie's RAG thanks you!

en: Build a filtered dict first: `{n: m for n, m in models.items() if m['params_m'] <= max_params_m}`.
Use `max()` with a `key` function to rank by score: `max(filtered, key=lambda n: filtered[n]['mteb'])`.
Iterating over a dict gives you its keys (the model names) â€” so `max()` over the filtered dict already returns a name, not a score.

instruction.en: MTEB's overall average treats every task category equally â€” but a RAG system cares mostly about Retrieval. Complete `weighted_score` so it returns the sum of each category's score multiplied by its weight. Then compare the retrieval-weighted score against the plain average and see how the ranking changes.

en: Loop over `categories.items()` and look up each category's weight with `weights[name]`.
You can do it in one line: `sum(score * weights[name] for name, score in categories.items())`.
0.6*54.2 + 0.2*82.1 + 0.1*75.9 + 0.1*46.1 = 61.14 â€” a RAG-weighted view scores this model lower than its plain average (64.58), because its Retrieval column is weak.
